abstract: Introduction. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is characterised by progressive fibrosis and inflammation. Preclinical models of these processes translate poorly to human CKD. Animal models are limited by species differences, while two-dimensional cultures and organoids do not reproduce the three-dimensional, multicellular environment of the human kidney. We sought to develop and characterise precision-cut human kidney slices (PCKS) as an ex-vivo platform for studying renal disease and testing therapeutics. Methods. PCKS were prepared from human donor kidneys not utilised for transplantation and cultured in a proprietary bioreactor for up to six days. Tissue integrity, fibrogenesis, inflammation, lipid handling, and drug-induced injury were assessed by histology, digital pathology, secreted protein quantification, mass spectrometry-based lipidomics, and bulk RNA sequencing, with and without pharmacological intervention. Results. PCKS retained native cortical architecture and viability throughout culture. Slices underwent spontaneous, time-dependent fibrogenesis that was enhanced by transforming growth factor beta 1, abrogated by an ALK5 inhibitor, and attenuated by nintedanib but not pirfenidone. Single-fibre digital pathology resolved treatment-dependent changes in collagen content, morphology and architecture. Proinflammatory stimuli induced stimulus-selective cytokine and chemokine secretion through NF-{kappa}B, which was suppressed by an IKK2 inhibitor. Fatty acid treatment reproduced features of fatty kidney disease, including triacylglycerol accumulation and dose-dependent inflammation, while nephrotoxic drugs produced characteristic injury detectable across multiple longitudinal readouts. Conclusions. Human PCKS maintain renal architecture and viability ex-vivo and reproduce fibrotic, inflammatory, metabolic, and toxic responses at transcriptomic, proteomic and lipidomic scales. PCKS provide a physiologically relevant, human-based platform for renal disease modeling and drug discovery.
